newsitem.title: USA: US says trade panel not fit to referee Cuba row.
newsitem.headline: US says trade panel not fit to referee Cuba row.

text.p: The United States on Thursday challenged the World Trade Organisation's fitness to adjudicate a dispute over U.S. sanctions on Cuba and said it would not cooperate with a WTO investigative panel.

Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, in a statement, expressed disappointment at the WTO's intervention into its dispute with the European Union over the U.S. Helms-Burton law aimed at curbing foreign investment in Cuba.

Eizenstat said Washington would try to settle its differences with the EU directly but would not cooperate with the WTO panel. "The WTO is not an appropriate forum for resolving differences over what is essentially a disagreement over foreign policy," he said.

"The United States wishes to provide every opportunity to settle our differences with the EU in the dispute," Eizenstat's statement said. "We have been in intense discussions with the EU and agree with the characterisation today by (EU Trade Commissioner) Sir Leon Brittan that we have made 'good progress' regarding the dispute."
Brittan said in a statement in Geneva on Thursday that progress had been made in the talks with Washington and the EU still wanted a negotiated settlement.

Eizenstat added that if no prompt settlement were reached, Washington would formally advise the director-general of the WTO of its views and "we will make clear that the panel established today has no competence to proceed because this is matter of U.S. national security and foreign policy."
A U.S. official told reporters: "The United States is willing to go the last mile to try to reach a reasonable mutually agreeable settlement (with the EU)."

Elaborating on the Eizenstat statement, the official made the case that U.S. policy toward Cuba had been in place for nearly 40 years. Washington felt the EU position challenged not just the Helms-Burton law but the whole U.S. policy.

Helms-Burton, enacted in 1996 after Cuba shot down two small U.S. civilian aircraft and killed four Cuban-Americans, enshrined existing U.S. policy toward Cuba and toughened the embargo by threatening foreign investors dealing with U.S. properties confiscated by Cuba.
One of the authors of the controversial law, Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, said he was pleased by the U.S. position in the dispute.
"The administration and Congress are in complete agreement: WTO is not competenet to judge American foreign policy," Helms said in a statement.

U.S. officials say the Cuba sanctions policy is legal under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the set of open trading rules that underpins the WTO. Washington cites GATT's Article XXI on "Security Exceptions," which says nothing in the accord should prevent a signatory "from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests."
EU members and other U.S. trading partners challenge this U.S. interpretation and say Washington's use of the security exception in this case is not legitimate.
The statement read by Eizenstat said the U.S. stance was not motivated by a desire to gain commercially at the expense of other countries.
"Indeed, the opposite is true. We have been willing to pay the economic price for our principles even while firms from other countries have willingly stepped in to do business in Cuba," he said.
